structured_data.description:
In 2010, the United States Mint introduced a landmark coin program celebrating America’s most treasured national parks, monuments, and forests. Authorized by Congress under the America’s Beautiful National Parks Quarter Dollar Coin Act of 2008, this series honors the natural beauty and historic landmarks that define the nation.



Commonly referred to as the America the Beautiful (ATB) series, this program consists of 56 unique coin designs. Between 2010 and 2020, the U.S. Mint released five new designs each year, followed by a single final release in 2021. The complete series represents all 50 U.S. states, five U.S. territories, and the District of Columbia. Coins were released in the order of the historical establishment of the featured park, monument, or forest.



Each year’s coins were struck by both the Philadelphia Mint and the Denver Mint, and were produced in multiple formats, including bullion, uncirculated, and proof varieties. When ordering, designs, mint marks, and finishes are selected at random based on current inventory.







Design of 5 Oz Silver Coin - America the Beautiful ATB Random Years







The United States Mint is renowned for its craftsmanship, but the America the Beautiful 5 oz silver coins represent one of its most ambitious and visually striking programs. These coins showcase America’s natural and historical heritage on an unprecedented scale.



The obverse features a design inspired by the classic U.S. quarter-dollar, displaying George Washington, along with the inscriptions “LIBERTY,” “IN GOD WE TRUST,” and “UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.” While the layout is familiar, these coins stand apart due to their substantial 5 troy ounce silver weight and extraordinary thickness, making them far larger and heavier than a standard quarter.



The reverse showcases a highly detailed depiction of a specific national park, monument, or forest. The name of the site appears at the top of the coin, with the year of issue at the bottom. The state or territory is listed to the left of the date, while the historic inscription “E PLURIBUS UNUM” appears to the right.
